open_obligations: Note that neither odds ratio is statistically significant.
Check which group's priors are inaccurate on each claim.
Check who the participants were and whether they had any judge training; the cited passage calls them only participants, whereas Michael et al. ask for human judges to be evaluated and trained.

Note that Rahman et al. group judges by belief orientation (mainstream versus skeptical), not by strength of prior; check whether either group's priors are strong, as in Michael et al.'s open problem.
in.other_title: Prior-belief effects on accuracy: consultancy vs debate odds ratios
in.rationale: Michael et al. call for evaluating debate where judges have strong inaccurate priors. Rahman et al. report that under consultancy mainstream-prior judges were less accurate than skeptical ones (OR 0.70, p = 0.11), while under debate accuracy was nearly identical across prior groups (OR 1.10, p = 0.66); neither odds ratio is significant.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate still works when judges hold differing prior beliefs (mainstream versus skeptical), for COVID-19 claims

open_obligations: Check that Michael et al.'s open question concerns strong inaccurate priors, while the authors describe their human judges as having varying prior beliefs
Confirm whether the debaters here are GPT-4o rather than humans and whether Michael et al.'s main result used human debaters; neither cited passage names the debaters

Only the human-judge results bear on Michael et al.'s open problem, which concerns human judges; the LLM judges with and without simulated personas are not human judges. Michael et al. also ask for judges to be trained, and the cited passage describes no judge training.
in.other_title: Gap in prior debate work, including reference [36], on judges with strong prior beliefs
in.rationale: The authors cite prior work showing effectiveness even with unreliable experts [30, 31, 36], including Michael et al. [36], say that prior work largely ignores scenarios where judges exhibit cognitive biases or hold strong prior beliefs, and state that their work addresses this limitation by investigating whether debate remains effective when judges have existing cognitive biases about controversial topics. Michael et al. list cognitive biases and strong priors as an open problem, saying human judges should be evaluated and trained on questions where they have strong inaccurate priors, so the source ADDRESSES the target's open question.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: Whether debate remains effective when judges hold cognitive biases or strong prior beliefs about controversial topics; tested with human judges of varying prior beliefs and with LLM judges with and without simulated personas

text: Among the open problems for trustworthy AI debate, the authors state that human judges should be evaluated and trained on hard questions that exploit cognitive or social biases, where judges have strong inaccurate priors, or where the validity of evidence is hard to evaluate, to make sure debate works in such settings.
title: Does debate still work when judges hold strong inaccurate priors or cognitive biases?
